case_info.scenario: Two brothers, aged 69 and 76 years, were independently referred to our center in the same week for evaluation of a right olfactory cleft tumor that had been progressively developing over several years. The brothers had not been in contact with each other for many years. Neither had a history of chronic rhinosinusitis. The 69-year-old patient had a medical history of benign prostatic hypertrophy and prior septoplasty. The 76-year-old brother had no relevant medical or surgical history. Both brothers reported an ipsilateral nasal obstruction, with no other significant symptoms. Clinical examination on both patients revealed a lesion originating from the right olfactory cleft. Imaging studies were performed to further characterize the findings. A computed tomography scan demonstrated bilateral masses causing widening of the olfactory clefts, with the right-sided lesion being larger than the left and causing nasal bone thinning in both patients (Figure 1). Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a smooth, larger, right-sided lesion in the olfactory clefts with heterogeneous T2 signal and heterogenous contrast enhancement, along with a smaller lesion on the left side.
case_info.caption: Computed tomography (CT) images of 2 brothers with bilateral lesions in the olfactory clefts. A, Cone-beam CT in the 69-year-old brother demonstrated significant widening of the olfactory clefts and right-sided bony thinning. B, Reformatted conventional CT scan in the 76-year-old brother showed similar findings.
case_info.explanation: After initial evaluation and imaging, both patients underwent surgical resection of the tumor in the right olfactory cleft to improve their nasal breathing and for pathological examination. A biopsy of the lesion located in the left olfactory cleft for both patients was also performed. Pathological examination revealed a similar finding in both brothers: a polypoid formation with dystrophic respiratory glands, sometimes with intestinal metaplasia and sometimes with ciliated lining, anarchically distributed within the chorion, without adenomatous or atypical character. This histopathological presentation strongly supports the diagnosis of respiratory epithelial adenomatoid hamartoma (REAH), despite the absence of genetic analysis.1,2 Olfactory cleft hamartomas are benign tumors that may be isolated or associated with chronic rhinosinusitis. They typically appear as a smooth polypoid mass in the anterior part of the nasal cavity. These lesions predominantly affect men, with a male to female ratio of 7:2.2The olfactory cleft is the most common site for hamartoma, followed by the posterior region of the septum. Both nasal cavities are involved in most cases (53%).3On imaging, hamartomas are usually seen as exophytic polypoid homogeneous lesions with smooth expansion of the olfactory cleft without bony erosion and exhibiting a characteristic crescentic half-moon appearance on the sagittal views when the lesion is situated along the olfactory cleft.4 The 5th World Health Organization Classification identifies 3 types of hamartomas: REAH, seromucinous hamartoma, and nasal chondromesenchymal hamartoma (CMH). Pathological examination and molecular analysis are essential for differentiation, as REAH and seromucinous hamartoma cannot be distinguished based on imaging alone. CMHs are usually found in infants and contain mixed mesenchymal elements, including cartilage. CMH can be associated with aDICER1(tumor-suppressor gene) variant.4,5 There is currently no cause identified for isolated REAH, but research is limited. Some evidence suggests that hamartomas may arise secondary to inflammatory processes, such as chronic rhinosinusitis.3A congenital cause is also suspected, but no genetic basis has been identified yet. It is quite rare to see similar isolated REAH in 2 brothers without any associated inflammatory conditions. This clinical case raises the possibility of an unknown underlying genetic mechanism. Treatment is symptom dependent. Surgical removal is often performed in cases of nasal obstruction or to restore olfactory function, with a high success rate and a low risk of recurrence.1,3While surgery is not always necessary, a biopsy is recommended when imaging findings are inconclusive to rule out other potential diagnoses. Differentials diagnosis include Schneiderian papilloma, sinonasal adenocarcinoma, or olfactory neuroblastoma. Imaging often helps to differentiate REAH from other diagnoses. In chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, nasal polyps typically originate from the ethmoid sinuses, whereas the imaging here clearly shows a lesion widening the olfactory cleft (Figure 2). Schneiderian papillomas are rarely bilateral and typically exhibit a more irregular or lobulated appearance on T2-weighted imaging, often accompanied by bone remodeling at the attachment point or bone erosion—features that are absent in this case. Malignant tumors, such as ethmoid sinus adenocarcinoma, typically demonstrate aggressive characteristics, including bone destruction, heterogeneous enhancement, and invasion of adjacent structures, none of which were observed here. Finally, encephaloceles are characterized by herniation of intracranial contents into the nasal cavity and are commonly associated with skull base defects, which are not identified in these images.

       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We

       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the

   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an

case_info.caption: Computed tomography (CT) images of 2 brothers with bilateral lesions in the olfactory clefts. A, Cone-beam CT in the 69-year-old brother demonstrated significant widening of the olfactory clefts and right-sided bony thinning. B, Reformatted conventional CT scan in the 76-year-old brother showed similar findings.
case_info.explanation: After initial evaluation and imaging, both patients underwent surgical resection of the tumor in the right olfactory cleft to improve their nasal breathing and for pathological examination. A biopsy of the lesion located in the left olfactory cleft for both patients was also performed. Pathological examination revealed a similar finding in both brothers: a polypoid formation with dystrophic respiratory glands, sometimes with intestinal metaplasia and sometimes with ciliated lining, anarchically distributed within the chorion, without adenomatous or atypical character. This histopathological presentation strongly supports the diagnosis of respiratory epithelial adenomatoid hamartoma (REAH), despite the absence of genetic analysis.1,2 Olfactory cleft hamartomas are benign tumors that may be isolated or associated with chronic rhinosinusitis. They typically appear as a smooth polypoid mass in the anterior part of the nasal cavity. These lesions predominantly affect men, with a male to female ratio of 7:2.2The olfactory cleft is the most common site for hamartoma, followed by the posterior region of the septum. Both nasal cavities are involved in most cases (53%).3On imaging, hamartomas are usually seen as exophytic polypoid homogeneous lesions with smooth expansion of the olfactory cleft without bony erosion and exhibiting a characteristic crescentic half-moon appearance on the sagittal views when the lesion is situated along the olfactory cleft.4 The 5th World Health Organization Classification identifies 3 types of hamartomas: REAH, seromucinous hamartoma, and nasal chondromesenchymal hamartoma (CMH). Pathological examination and molecular analysis are essential for differentiation, as REAH and seromucinous hamartoma cannot be distinguished based on imaging alone. CMHs are usually found in infants and contain mixed mesenchymal elements, including cartilage. CMH can be associated with aDICER1(tumor-suppressor gene) variant.4,5 There is currently no cause identified for isolated REAH, but research is limited. Some evidence suggests that hamartomas may arise secondary to inflammatory processes, such as chronic rhinosinusitis.3A congenital cause is also suspected, but no genetic basis has been identified yet. It is quite rare to see similar isolated REAH in 2 brothers without any associated inflammatory conditions. This clinical case raises the possibility of an unknown underlying genetic mechanism. Treatment is symptom dependent. Surgical removal is often performed in cases of nasal obstruction or to restore olfactory function, with a high success rate and a low risk of recurrence.1,3While surgery is not always necessary, a biopsy is recommended when imaging findings are inconclusive to rule out other potential diagnoses. Differentials diagnosis include Schneiderian papilloma, sinonasal adenocarcinoma, or olfactory neuroblastoma. Imaging often helps to differentiate REAH from other diagnoses. In chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, nasal polyps typically originate from the ethmoid sinuses, whereas the imaging here clearly shows a lesion widening the olfactory cleft (Figure 2). Schneiderian papillomas are rarely bilateral and typically exhibit a more irregular or lobulated appearance on T2-weighted imaging, often accompanied by bone remodeling at the attachment point or bone erosion—features that are absent in this case. Malignant tumors, such as ethmoid sinus adenocarcinoma, typically demonstrate aggressive characteristics, including bone destruction, heterogeneous enhancement, and invasion of adjacent structures, none of which were observed here. Finally, encephaloceles are characterized by herniation of intracranial contents into the nasal cavity and are commonly associated with skull base defects, which are not identified in these images.

A, Cone-beam CT in the 69-year-old brother demonstrated significant widening of the olfactory clefts and right-sided bony thinning. case_info.explanation: After initial evaluation and imaging, both patients underwent surgical resection of the tumor in the right olfactory cleft to improve their nasal breathing and for pathological examination. A biopsy of the lesion located in the left olfactory cleft for both patients was also performed. Pathological examination revealed a similar finding in both brothers: a polypoid formation with dystrophic respiratory glands, sometimes with intestinal metaplasia and sometimes with ciliated lining, anarchically distributed within the chorion, without adenomatous or atypical character. This histopathological presentation strongly supports the diagnosis of respiratory epithelial adenomatoid hamartoma (REAH), despite the absence of genetic analysis.1,2 Olfactory cleft hamartomas are benign tumors that may be isolated or associated with chronic rhinosinusitis. They typically appear as a smooth polypoid mass in the anterior part of the nasal cavity. These lesions predominantly affect men, with a male to female ratio of 7:2.2The olfactory cleft is the most common site for hamartoma, followed by the posterior region of the septum. Both nasal cavities are involved in most cases (53%).3On imaging, hamartomas are usually seen as exophytic polypoid homogeneous lesions with smooth expansion of the olfactory cleft without bony erosion and exhibiting a characteristic crescentic half-moon appearance on the sagittal views when the lesion is situated along the olfactory cleft.4 The 5th World Health Organization Classification identifies 3 types of hamartomas: REAH, seromucinous hamartoma, and nasal chondromesenchymal hamartoma (CMH). Pathological examination and molecular analysis are essential for differentiation, as REAH and seromucinous hamartoma cannot be distinguished based on imaging alone. CMHs are usually found in infants and contain mixed mesenchymal elements, including cartilage. CMH can be associated with aDICER1(tumor-suppressor gene) variant.4,5 There is currently no cause identified for isolated REAH, but research is limited. Some evidence suggests that hamartomas may arise secondary to inflammatory processes, such as chronic rhinosinusitis.3A congenital cause is also suspected, but no genetic basis has been identified yet. It is quite rare to see similar isolated REAH in 2 brothers without any associated inflammatory conditions. This clinical case raises the possibility of an unknown underlying genetic mechanism. Treatment is symptom dependent. Surgical removal is often performed in cases of nasal obstruction or to restore olfactory function, with a high success rate and a low risk of recurrence.1,3While surgery is not always necessary, a biopsy is recommended when imaging findings are inconclusive to rule out other potential diagnoses. Differentials diagnosis include Schneiderian papilloma, sinonasal adenocarcinoma, or olfactory neuroblastoma. Imaging often helps to differentiate REAH from other diagnoses. In chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, nasal polyps typically originate from the ethmoid sinuses, whereas the imaging here clearly shows a lesion widening the olfactory cleft (Figure 2). Schneiderian papillomas are rarely bilateral and typically exhibit a more irregular or lobulated appearance on T2-weighted imaging, often accompanied by bone remodeling at the attachment point or bone erosion—features that are absent in this case. Malignant tumors, such as ethmoid sinus adenocarcinoma, typically demonstrate aggressive characteristics, including bone destruction, heterogeneous enhancement, and invasion of adjacent structures, none of which were observed here. Finally, encephaloceles are characterized by herniation of intracranial contents into the nasal cavity and are commonly associated with skull base defects, which are not identified in these images.

case_info.explanation: After initial evaluation and imaging, both patients underwent surgical resection of the tumor in the right olfactory cleft to improve their nasal breathing and for pathological examination. A biopsy of the lesion located in the left olfactory cleft for both patients was also performed. Pathological examination revealed a similar finding in both brothers: a polypoid formation with dystrophic respiratory glands, sometimes with intestinal metaplasia and sometimes with ciliated lining, anarchically distributed within the chorion, without adenomatous or atypical character. This histopathological presentation strongly supports the diagnosis of respiratory epithelial adenomatoid hamartoma (REAH), despite the absence of genetic analysis.1,2 Olfactory cleft hamartomas are benign tumors that may be isolated or associated with chronic rhinosinusitis. They typically appear as a smooth polypoid mass in the anterior part of the nasal cavity. These lesions predominantly affect men, with a male to female ratio of 7:2.2The olfactory cleft is the most common site for hamartoma, followed by the posterior region of the septum. Both nasal cavities are involved in most cases (53%).3On imaging, hamartomas are usually seen as exophytic polypoid homogeneous lesions with smooth expansion of the olfactory cleft without bony erosion and exhibiting a characteristic crescentic half-moon appearance on the sagittal views when the lesion is situated along the olfactory cleft.4 The 5th World Health Organization Classification identifies 3 types of hamartomas: REAH, seromucinous hamartoma, and nasal chondromesenchymal hamartoma (CMH). Pathological examination and molecular analysis are essential for differentiation, as REAH and seromucinous hamartoma cannot be distinguished based on imaging alone. CMHs are usually found in infants and contain mixed mesenchymal elements, including cartilage. CMH can be associated with aDICER1(tumor-suppressor gene) variant.4,5 There is currently no cause identified for isolated REAH, but research is limited. Some evidence suggests that hamartomas may arise secondary to inflammatory processes, such as chronic rhinosinusitis.3A congenital cause is also suspected, but no genetic basis has been identified yet. It is quite rare to see similar isolated REAH in 2 brothers without any associated inflammatory conditions. This clinical case raises the possibility of an unknown underlying genetic mechanism. Treatment is symptom dependent. Surgical removal is often performed in cases of nasal obstruction or to restore olfactory function, with a high success rate and a low risk of recurrence.1,3While surgery is not always necessary, a biopsy is recommended when imaging findings are inconclusive to rule out other potential diagnoses. Differentials diagnosis include Schneiderian papilloma, sinonasal adenocarcinoma, or olfactory neuroblastoma. Imaging often helps to differentiate REAH from other diagnoses. In chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, nasal polyps typically originate from the ethmoid sinuses, whereas the imaging here clearly shows a lesion widening the olfactory cleft (Figure 2). Schneiderian papillomas are rarely bilateral and typically exhibit a more irregular or lobulated appearance on T2-weighted imaging, often accompanied by bone remodeling at the attachment point or bone erosion—features that are absent in this case. Malignant tumors, such as ethmoid sinus adenocarcinoma, typically demonstrate aggressive characteristics, including bone destruction, heterogeneous enhancement, and invasion of adjacent structures, none of which were observed here. case_info.explanation: After initial evaluation and imaging, both patients underwent surgical resection of the tumor in the right olfactory cleft to improve their nasal breathing and for pathological examination. A biopsy of the lesion located in the left olfactory cleft for both patients was also performed. Pathological examination revealed a similar finding in both brothers: a polypoid formation with dystrophic respiratory glands, sometimes with intestinal metaplasia and sometimes with ciliated lining, anarchically distributed within the chorion, without adenomatous or atypical character. This histopathological presentation strongly supports the diagnosis of respiratory epithelial adenomatoid hamartoma (REAH), despite the absence of genetic analysis.1,2 Olfactory cleft hamartomas are benign tumors that may be isolated or associated with chronic rhinosinusitis. They typically appear as a smooth polypoid mass in the anterior part of the nasal cavity. These lesions predominantly affect men, with a male to female ratio of 7:2.2The olfactory cleft is the most common site for hamartoma, followed by the posterior region of the septum. Both nasal cavities are involved in most cases (53%).3On imaging, hamartomas are usually seen as exophytic polypoid homogeneous lesions with smooth expansion of the olfactory cleft without bony erosion and exhibiting a characteristic crescentic half-moon appearance on the sagittal views when the lesion is situated along the olfactory cleft.4 The 5th World Health Organization Classification identifies 3 types of hamartomas: REAH, seromucinous hamartoma, and nasal chondromesenchymal hamartoma (CMH). Pathological examination and molecular analysis are essential for differentiation, as REAH and seromucinous hamartoma cannot be distinguished based on imaging alone. CMHs are usually found in infants and contain mixed mesenchymal elements, including cartilage. CMH can be associated with aDICER1(tumor-suppressor gene) variant.4,5 There is currently no cause identified for isolated REAH, but research is limited. Some evidence suggests that hamartomas may arise secondary to inflammatory processes, such as chronic rhinosinusitis.3A congenital cause is also suspected, but no genetic basis has been identified yet. It is quite rare to see similar isolated REAH in 2 brothers without any associated inflammatory conditions. This clinical case raises the possibility of an unknown underlying genetic mechanism. Treatment is symptom dependent. Surgical removal is often performed in cases of nasal obstruction or to restore olfactory function, with a high success rate and a low risk of recurrence.1,3While surgery is not always necessary, a biopsy is recommended when imaging findings are inconclusive to rule out other potential diagnoses. Differentials diagnosis include Schneiderian papilloma, sinonasal adenocarcinoma, or olfactory neuroblastoma. Imaging often helps to differentiate REAH from other diagnoses. Malignant tumors, such as ethmoid sinus adenocarcinoma, typically demonstrate aggressive characteristics, including bone destruction, heterogeneous enhancement, and invasion of adjacent structures, none of which were observed here. Finally, encephaloceles are characterized by herniation of intracranial contents into the nasal cavity and are commonly associated with skull base defects, which are not identified in these images.

case_info.explanation: After initial evaluation and imaging, both patients underwent surgical resection of the tumor in the right olfactory cleft to improve their nasal breathing and for pathological examination. A biopsy of the lesion located in the left olfactory cleft for both patients was also performed. Pathological examination revealed a similar finding in both brothers: a polypoid formation with dystrophic respiratory glands, sometimes with intestinal metaplasia and sometimes with ciliated lining, anarchically distributed within the chorion, without adenomatous or atypical character. This histopathological presentation strongly supports the diagnosis of respiratory epithelial adenomatoid hamartoma (REAH), despite the absence of genetic analysis.1,2 Olfactory cleft hamartomas are benign tumors that may be isolated or associated with chronic rhinosinusitis. They typically appear as a smooth polypoid mass in the anterior part of the nasal cavity. These lesions predominantly affect men, with a male to female ratio of 7:2.2The olfactory cleft is the most common site for hamartoma, followed by the posterior region of the septum. Both nasal cavities are involved in most cases (53%).3On imaging, hamartomas are usually seen as exophytic polypoid homogeneous lesions with smooth expansion of the olfactory cleft without bony erosion and exhibiting a characteristic crescentic half-moon appearance on the sagittal views when the lesion is situated along the olfactory cleft.4 The 5th World Health Organization Classification identifies 3 types of hamartomas: REAH, seromucinous hamartoma, and nasal chondromesenchymal hamartoma (CMH). Pathological examination and molecular analysis are essential for differentiation, as REAH and seromucinous hamartoma cannot be distinguished based on imaging alone. CMHs are usually found in infants and contain mixed mesenchymal elements, including cartilage. CMH can be associated with aDICER1(tumor-suppressor gene) variant.4,5 There is currently no cause identified for isolated REAH, but research is limited. Some evidence suggests that hamartomas may arise secondary to inflammatory processes, such as chronic rhinosinusitis.3A congenital cause is also suspected, but no genetic basis has been identified yet. It is quite rare to see similar isolated REAH in 2 brothers without any associated inflammatory conditions. This clinical case raises the possibility of an unknown underlying genetic mechanism. Treatment is symptom dependent. Surgical removal is often performed in cases of nasal obstruction or to restore olfactory function, with a high success rate and a low risk of recurrence.1,3While surgery is not always necessary, a biopsy is recommended when imaging findings are inconclusive to rule out other potential diagnoses. Differentials diagnosis include Schneiderian papilloma, sinonasal adenocarcinoma, or olfactory neuroblastoma. Imaging often helps to differentiate REAH from other diagnoses. In chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, nasal polyps typically originate from the ethmoid sinuses, whereas the imaging here clearly shows a lesion widening the olfactory cleft (Figure 2). Schneiderian papillomas are rarely bilateral and typically exhibit a more irregular or lobulated appearance on T2-weighted imaging, often accompanied by bone remodeling at the attachment point or bone erosion—features that are absent in this case. Malignant tumors, such as ethmoid sinus adenocarcinoma, typically demonstrate aggressive characteristics, including bone destruction, heterogeneous enhancement, and invasion of adjacent structures, none of which were observed here. Finally, encephaloceles are characterized by herniation of intracranial contents into the nasal cavity and are commonly associated with skull base defects, which are not identified in these images.

case_info.explanation: After initial evaluation and imaging, both patients underwent surgical resection of the tumor in the right olfactory cleft to improve their nasal breathing and for pathological examination. A biopsy of the lesion located in the left olfactory cleft for both patients was also performed. Pathological examination revealed a similar finding in both brothers: a polypoid formation with dystrophic respiratory glands, sometimes with intestinal metaplasia and sometimes with ciliated lining, anarchically distributed within the chorion, without adenomatous or atypical character. This histopathological presentation strongly supports the diagnosis of respiratory epithelial adenomatoid hamartoma (REAH), despite the absence of genetic analysis.1,2 Olfactory cleft hamartomas are benign tumors that may be isolated or associated with chronic rhinosinusitis. They typically appear as a smooth polypoid mass in the anterior part of the nasal cavity. These lesions predominantly affect men, with a male to female ratio of 7:2.2The olfactory cleft is the most common site for hamartoma, followed by the posterior region of the septum. Both nasal cavities are involved in most cases (53%).3On imaging, hamartomas are usually seen as exophytic polypoid homogeneous lesions with smooth expansion of the olfactory cleft without bony erosion and exhibiting a characteristic crescentic half-moon appearance on the sagittal views when the lesion is situated along the olfactory cleft.4 The 5th World Health Organization Classification identifies 3 types of hamartomas: REAH, seromucinous hamartoma, and nasal chondromesenchymal hamartoma (CMH). Pathological examination and molecular analysis are essential for differentiation, as REAH and seromucinous hamartoma cannot be distinguished based on imaging alone. CMHs are usually found in infants and contain mixed mesenchymal elements, including cartilage. CMH can be associated with aDICER1(tumor-suppressor gene) variant.4,5 There is currently no cause identified for isolated REAH, but research is limited. Some evidence suggests that hamartomas may arise secondary to inflammatory processes, such as chronic rhinosinusitis.3A congenital cause is also suspected, but no genetic basis has been identified yet. It is quite rare to see similar isolated REAH in 2 brothers without any associated inflammatory conditions. This clinical case raises the possibility of an unknown underlying genetic mechanism. Treatment is symptom dependent. Surgical removal is often performed in cases of nasal obstruction or to restore olfactory function, with a high success rate and a low risk of recurrence.1,3While surgery is not always necessary, a biopsy is recommended when imaging findings are inconclusive to rule out other potential diagnoses. Differentials diagnosis include Schneiderian papilloma, sinonasal adenocarcinoma, or olfactory neuroblastoma. Imaging often helps to differentiate REAH from other diagnoses. In chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, nasal polyps typically originate from the ethmoid sinuses, whereas the imaging here clearly shows a lesion widening the olfactory cleft (Figure 2). Schneiderian papillomas are rarely bilateral and typically exhibit a more irregular or lobulated appearance on T2-weighted imaging, often accompanied by bone remodeling at the attachment point or bone erosion—features that are absent in this case. Malignant tumors, such as ethmoid sinus adenocarcinoma, typically demonstrate aggressive characteristics, including bone destruction, heterogeneous enhancement, and invasion of adjacent structures, none of which were observed here. Finally, encephaloceles are characterized by herniation of intracranial contents into the nasal cavity and are commonly associated with skull base defects, which are not identified in these images.

case_info.scenario: Two brothers, aged 69 and 76 years, were independently referred to our center in the same week for evaluation of a right olfactory cleft tumor that had been progressively developing over several years. The brothers had not been in contact with each other for many years. Neither had a history of chronic rhinosinusitis. The 69-year-old patient had a medical history of benign prostatic hypertrophy and prior septoplasty. The 76-year-old brother had no relevant medical or surgical history. Both brothers reported an ipsilateral nasal obstruction, with no other significant symptoms. Clinical examination on both patients revealed a lesion originating from the right olfactory cleft. Imaging studies were performed to further characterize the findings. A computed tomography scan demonstrated bilateral masses causing widening of the olfactory clefts, with the right-sided lesion being larger than the left and causing nasal bone thinning in both patients (Figure 1). Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a smooth, larger, right-sided lesion in the olfactory clefts with heterogeneous T2 signal and heterogenous contrast enhancement, along with a smaller lesion on the left side.
case_info.caption: Computed tomography (CT) images of 2 brothers with bilateral lesions in the olfactory clefts. A, Cone-beam CT in the 69-year-old brother demonstrated significant widening of the olfactory clefts and right-sided bony thinning. B, Reformatted conventional CT scan in the 76-year-old brother showed similar findings.
case_info.explanation: After initial evaluation and imaging, both patients underwent surgical resection of the tumor in the right olfactory cleft to improve their nasal breathing and for pathological examination. A biopsy of the lesion located in the left olfactory cleft for both patients was also performed. Pathological examination revealed a similar finding in both brothers: a polypoid formation with dystrophic respiratory glands, sometimes with intestinal metaplasia and sometimes with ciliated lining, anarchically distributed within the chorion, without adenomatous or atypical character. This histopathological presentation strongly supports the diagnosis of respiratory epithelial adenomatoid hamartoma (REAH), despite the absence of genetic analysis.1,2 Olfactory cleft hamartomas are benign tumors that may be isolated or associated with chronic rhinosinusitis. They typically appear as a smooth polypoid mass in the anterior part of the nasal cavity. These lesions predominantly affect men, with a male to female ratio of 7:2.2The olfactory cleft is the most common site for hamartoma, followed by the posterior region of the septum. Both nasal cavities are involved in most cases (53%).3On imaging, hamartomas are usually seen as exophytic polypoid homogeneous lesions with smooth expansion of the olfactory cleft without bony erosion and exhibiting a characteristic crescentic half-moon appearance on the sagittal views when the lesion is situated along the olfactory cleft.4 The 5th World Health Organization Classification identifies 3 types of hamartomas: REAH, seromucinous hamartoma, and nasal chondromesenchymal hamartoma (CMH). Pathological examination and molecular analysis are essential for differentiation, as REAH and seromucinous hamartoma cannot be distinguished based on imaging alone. CMHs are usually found in infants and contain mixed mesenchymal elements, including cartilage. CMH can be associated with aDICER1(tumor-suppressor gene) variant.4,5 There is currently no cause identified for isolated REAH, but research is limited. Some evidence suggests that hamartomas may arise secondary to inflammatory processes, such as chronic rhinosinusitis.3A congenital cause is also suspected, but no genetic basis has been identified yet. It is quite rare to see similar isolated REAH in 2 brothers without any associated inflammatory conditions. This clinical case raises the possibility of an unknown underlying genetic mechanism. Treatment is symptom dependent. Surgical removal is often performed in cases of nasal obstruction or to restore olfactory function, with a high success rate and a low risk of recurrence.1,3While surgery is not always necessary, a biopsy is recommended when imaging findings are inconclusive to rule out other potential diagnoses. Differentials diagnosis include Schneiderian papilloma, sinonasal adenocarcinoma, or olfactory neuroblastoma. Imaging often helps to differentiate REAH from other diagnoses. In chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, nasal polyps typically originate from the ethmoid sinuses, whereas the imaging here clearly shows a lesion widening the olfactory cleft (Figure 2). Schneiderian papillomas are rarely bilateral and typically exhibit a more irregular or lobulated appearance on T2-weighted imaging, often accompanied by bone remodeling at the attachment point or bone erosion—features that are absent in this case. Malignant tumors, such as ethmoid sinus adenocarcinoma, typically demonstrate aggressive characteristics, including bone destruction, heterogeneous enhancement, and invasion of adjacent structures, none of which were observed here. Finally, encephaloceles are characterized by herniation of intracranial contents into the nasal cavity and are commonly associated with skull base defects, which are not identified in these images.
